title: Atlas and Lantern
premise: In the river city of Bellhaven, on the eve of a revolution nobody has named yet, Hazel Okafor—apprentice clockmaker, unregistered orphan of mixed heritage—is summoned to repair the observatory's master clock, the city's official timekeeper. There they discover the clock's hidden ledger room, where a previous keeper recorded births, deaths, and debts the government never counted, including Hazel's own parents. When a census taker begins hunting unregistered residents to erase them from the record before the new regime's historians arrive, Hazel must decide whether to keep carrying their life in a satchel or to claim the ledger, the clock, and a found family of observatory misfits. The story ends on the morning the ice breaks: Hazel testifies before the victors' provisional council, enters the Okafor names into the restored ledger, and winds the master clock publicly for the first time in a generation—visible at last, and staying.
about_author: Jude Blackwood is a former museum conservator who spent six years cataloguing unclaimed heirlooms before turning to fiction. They write historical novels about people the paperwork forgot, and live in a house with too many clocks and exactly one working one.

chapters.title: The Weight of Small Things
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. In the workshop of Master Idris Okafor's old rival, Hazel packs their entire life into a satchel: tools, a broken watch, a forged apprenticeship paper. The census wagons are already on the bridge. The emotional beat is quiet dread dressed as routine—Hazel measures the world in what can be carried.

chapters.title: Summons
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. A city clerk delivers an official order: the observatory's master clock has stopped, and Hazel, cheapest available apprentice, is sent to fix it. Hazel hesitates—official paper is dangerous paper—but refusing marks them too. Beat: the trap and the opportunity arriving in the same envelope.

chapters.title: Nine Hundred Steps
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Hazel climbs the observatory tower and meets the keeper's daughter, Wren Aldous, who guards the stopped clock like a tomb. The mechanism is sabotaged, not broken. Beat: wonder curdling into suspicion—someone wanted time in Bellhaven to stop being official.

chapters.title: The Man Who Asked Twice
chapters.summary: Census taker Silas Crane's POV. Crane interviews workshop households, polite and meticulous, flagging anyone whose answers shift between visits. Hazel's name appears on his list twice with different details. Beat: cold professional satisfaction; the reader sees the hunt begin before the hunted do.

chapters.title: Escapement
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Repairing the escapement, Hazel finds a hidden door behind the clock's face: a ledger room, decades of records kept by Wren's father—births, debts, and unregistered people the state never counted. The last entry, in his hand: 'Okafor, Hazel. Born in the winter of the flood.' Beat: vertigo of being known.

chapters.title: What the Ledger Says
chapters.summary: Hazel and Wren's shared POV, alternating. Wren explains her father recorded what the government refused to: the erased, the mixed-heritage families, the debtors sold downstream. Hazel reads their parents' names. Beat: grief and inheritance arriving together—Hazel's identity was written down all along, by a stranger's kindness.

chapters.title: Ink and Ice
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren reveals the ledger's danger: when the new regime's historians arrive after the expected uprising, official records will be rewritten. Her father died keeping the true one. She asks Hazel to help copy and hide it before the river ice breaks. Beat: a request disguised as a job offer.

chapters.title: Apprentices of Nothing
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Hazel returns to the workshop and finds it sealed by census order; Master Idris has been taken 'for questioning.' Hazel sleeps in the observatory, technically employed, technically homeless. Beat: the cost of visibility arriving before any reward.

chapters.title: The Cook Who Counts
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. The observatory's cook, Marisol, an unregistered woman who has hidden in plain sight for twenty years, feeds Hazel and teaches them which neighbors can be trusted. Beat: warmth with edges—found family forming out of shared concealment.

chapters.title: Crane's Ledger
chapters.summary: Crane's POV. Crane cross-references his census lists with the old regime's tax rolls and notices the observatory employs a clockmaker who officially does not exist. He requests the master clock's maintenance logs. Beat: the net tightening with bureaucratic patience.

chapters.title: Gears Within Gears
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Restoring the clock, Hazel discovers Wren's father built a second, secret dial—one that only runs if the official mechanism does. The clock itself is an argument: true time and official time, geared together. Beat: Hazel begins to understand the ledger as machinery, not paper.

chapters.title: A Night of Small Treasons
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV. The observatory household—Wren, Marisol, the half-blind stargazer Old Piotr—share dinner and, one by one, their real names. Hazel says 'Okafor' aloud for the first time in years. Beat: found family crystallizing; the safest room in the city is the most exposed.

chapters.title: The Historians' Advance Party
chapters.summary: Crane's POV. A delegation of the incoming regime's historians arrives early, escorted by soldiers. Crane is ordered to deliver a complete census—'clean' of irregular persons—before the ice breaks. Beat: the stakes become historical, not just personal.

chapters.title: What Idris Carried
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Idris is released, broken, and confesses he sold out Hazel's parents' names to the census years ago to keep his workshop. He begs forgiveness. Beat: fury and pity tangled; Hazel learns that survival and betrayal can wear the same coat.

chapters.title: The Copying Nights
chapters.summary: Wren and Hazel's shared POV. By lamplight they copy the ledger, page by page, hiding duplicates in clock cases bound for other towns. Hazel's hands, built for fine work, learn the weight of other people's lives. Beat: intimacy through shared labor; love unspoken but load-bearing.

chapters.title: Crane Calls
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Crane visits the observatory, courteous, asking about the stopped clock and the 'unregistered apprentice' rumor. Hazel lies well—too well—and hates how easily it comes. Beat: the seduction and shame of invisibility.

chapters.title: Piotr's Stars
chapters.summary: Old Piotr's POV. The stargazer, who once calibrated the clock to the sky, reveals the observatory's basement holds his own archive: forty years of observations the state declared impossible. Beat: Hazel realizes they've joined a lineage of keepers, not an accident of shelter.

chapters.title: The Bridge at Dusk
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. Marisol is recognized on the bridge by a census clerk and barely escapes, thanks to a ferryman who owes the observatory. The household realizes Crane's net now touches everyone they love. Beat: fear going communal; hiding is no longer sustainable.

chapters.title: A Question Too Many
chapters.summary: Crane's POV. Crane interviews Hazel a third time and asks, softly, where Hazel's parents are buried. Hazel's pause answers him. Crane marks the page. Beat: the blurb's pivot—staying invisible was never really an option; the choice is only how to be seen.

chapters.title: The Broken Watch
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Hazel repairs their parents' watch, the one object carried from the old life, and winds it. Inside the case back: their mother's engraving—a name Hazel never knew was theirs. Beat: identity reclaimed in miniature; grief turning to resolve.

chapters.title: Terms of the Regime
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. The historians offer Wren a deal: surrender her father's 'anomalous records' and the observatory keeps funding. She stalls, asking for time. Beat: temptation with a civilized face; Wren nearly says yes.

chapters.title: What the River Keeps
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Hazel visits the flooded district where their parents died, guided by a ledger entry, and finds neighbors who remember them. An old woman gives Hazel a photograph. Beat: the past proving more solid than the papers said; belonging has witnesses.

chapters.title: Crane's Doubt
chapters.summary: Crane's POV. Ordered to certify the 'clean' census, Crane hesitates over the Okafor page—he has begun to suspect the historians will erase him too, eventually. Beat: the hunter's first crack; complicity discovering its own expiry date.

chapters.title: The Plan of Gears
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV. The household plans: restore the master clock publicly, enter the true ledger into the provisional council's record the moment the uprising's victors convene, and testify. Every role assigned, every duplicate hidden. Beat: hope becoming engineering—risky, scheduled, real.

chapters.title: Sabotage
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Someone destroys the clock's escapement a second time—Idris, coerced by Crane's men, or so it seems. Hazel finds a deliberate flaw only a clockmaker would leave: a message. Beat: betrayal and rescue in the same wound; trust tested at its weakest point.

chapters.title: Idris's Last Repair
chapters.summary: Idris's POV. Idris confesses the truth: he sabotaged the clock under threat, then built the flaw to leave a trail for whoever could read it. He gives Hazel his master's tools. Beat: a broken man's redemption priced in honesty; Hazel accepts it without absolution.

chapters.title: The Ice Cracks Early
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV. A warm wind; the river groans. The ice will break days ahead of schedule—before the copying is done, before the council convenes. Beat: time, the book's true antagonist, turning against them.

chapters.title: Crane Comes at Night
chapters.summary: Crane's POV. Crane raids the observatory with soldiers, seizing the visible ledger room. But the household has emptied it—except Wren, who stays behind to stall him. Beat: sacrifice as strategy; the reader fears the worst.

chapters.title: Wren's Bargain
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren trades Crane a convincing partial copy for Hazel's escape with the true ledger, letting herself be arrested as the 'keeper of anomalous records.' Beat: the inheritance defended at the cost of its keeper's freedom.

chapters.title: The Long Way Down
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Hazel carries the ledger down the nine hundred steps and across the cracking ice road to the provisional council's hall, pursued, guided by the ferryman. Beat: the carried life finally carried for others; terror and purpose indistinguishable.

chapters.title: The Council of the Victors
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Before the provisional council and the historians, Hazel opens the ledger and testifies: the erased names, their parents, the clock's true time. The historians object; the council wavers. Beat: climax of voice—one unregistered person making the record argue back.

chapters.title: What Crane Certifies
chapters.summary: Crane's POV. Called to verify, Crane must choose: certify his clean census or admit its forgery. He certifies the ledger's authenticity instead, damning himself. Beat: the antagonist's quiet defection; the record wins because even its enemy submits to it.

chapters.title: The Historians' Retreat
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, from custody. The historians, outmaneuvered, withdraw to negotiate; Wren is released into the crowd's custody. Beat: relief without triumph; the victors' memory is a thing still being built, not won.

chapters.title: Names on the Record
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Hazel enters the Okafor names, Marisol's, Piotr's, and Idris's into the ledger's new pages, then their own, in their own hand. Beat: the emotional summit—identity as an act, witnessed, irreversible.

chapters.title: Winding the Clock
chapters.summary: Ensemble POV. Before the city, Hazel restores the master clock and its secret dial together; true time and official time, geared as one, begin to move. The crowd counts the first strike. Beat: the book's central image fulfilled—keeping time as keeping faith.

chapters.title: What the Satchel Holds Now
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Hazel unpacks the satchel at last: tools on the bench, the watch on the mantel, the forged paper burned. The bag stays by the door, but empty by choice. Beat: carrying redefined—from hiding to readiness.

chapters.title: Idris at the Bench
chapters.summary: Idris's POV. Idris, pardoned but not forgiven, works under Hazel as journeyman, learning the ledger's history he once helped bury. Beat: inheritance flowing the wrong way, rightly; repair as ongoing work.

chapters.title: Crane's New Page
chapters.summary: Crane's POV. Crane, dismissed by the regime, applies to the council's archive as a clerk—the only work he knows—and is assigned, ironically, to Wren. Beat: ambiguous grace; the man who asked one question too many now answers them for a living.

chapters.title: The First Anniversary
chapters.summary: Wren and Hazel's shared POV. One year on: the observatory trains unregistered apprentices openly; the ledger grows; the ice breaks again on schedule. Hazel and Wren admit what the copying nights already knew. Beat: found family become institution; love recorded at last.

chapters.title: Atlas and Lantern
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Hazel teaches a new apprentice to measure the world—not in what can be carried, but in what can be kept, wound, and handed on. The master clock strikes; the ledger waits open. Beat: resolution as transmission—the atlas of names and the lantern of the record, passed forward.
